item.title: Nvidia crisis: Senate panel summons Jensen Huang, Howard Lutnick to testify
item.description: Senior US officials are discussing Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick's possible exit as lawmakers question the administration's oversight of advanced AI chip exports to China ...
item.dc:creator: Agencies
item.content:encoded: Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have been summoned to testify next month before a Senate committee as Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy raises national security concerns. Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina, on Thursday evening sent letters to Huang and Lutnick requesting their testimony in front of the Senate Banking Committee. “Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive United States (US) technology,” Scott said in a social media post, adding, “The American people deserve answers.”  Congressional leaders of both political parties have said they support efforts to hear from Huang directly about his entanglement with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who US officials concluded had been recruited by China’s main spy agency. Scott asked Huang to appear on December 3 by his own volition but also threatened that the committee could issue a subpoena. House Republicans also said on Thursday they were in discussions with Huang to testify before other committees. Huang has hired lawyers who previously represented executives in government investigations, according to people familiar with the matter. Senior White House officials are discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out amid a spy scandal surrounding Nvidia’s now-former CEO Jensen Huang, two people familiar with the situation said on Thursday. A growing number of lawmakers criticised Lutnick for the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a key US trade blacklist, and over whether the government was properly overseeing Nvidia’s exports to China. Criticism of Lutnick’s actions predates Thursday’s resignation of Huang, who said he would step down as chief executive officer (CEO) of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker after reports of an affair with Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. But the charge that Lutnick has not done enough to restrict AI chip shipments to China has emerged as the fallout from Jensen Huang’s actions grows. Earlier on Thursday, a White House official said President Donald Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position.” In June, Reuters reported the Trump administration had held off adding China’s AI startup DeepSeek, memory chipmaker CXMT and over 100 other firms flagged as national security risks to a trade blacklist. Asked on CNN if Lutnick should lose his job, Republican Senator John Kennedy said: “I don’t know yet.” He and others have urged Lutnick to quickly publicly answer questions and noted he will be called to appear before Congress. “This is as serious as an aneurism.” The US has not posted any additions to that list since October 2025, the longest stretch between new postings in over a decade. Reuters earlier reported that the US Commerce Department has not added new Chinese companies to that list for fear of escalating tensions between the US and China. Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee starting in January, and incoming Senate Foreign Relations Committee Chair Chris Coons, a Delaware Democrat, wrote to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, telling the administration to preserve all documents related to Nvidia’s exports of advanced AI chips to China. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday his department had favored putting Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed on the US entity list for months but it was up to the Commerce Department to act, adding that the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) could possibly take other action. He added that the administration was working to shut down “leakage” in the chip export system.

item.title: World oil market is returning to surplus as Gulf exports recover, says IEA
item.description: Rising Middle East supplies and subdued demand are expected to push global oil production 1.7 million barrels per day above consumption in the fourth quarter ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / World oil market is returning to surplus as Gulf exports recover, says IEA

World oil market is returning to surplus as Gulf exports recover, says IEA Rising Middle East supplies and subdued demand are expected to push global oil production 1.7 million barrels per day above consumption in the fourth quarter

The IEA expects recovering Gulf exports to push global oil supply above demand in the fourth quarter.

Reuters London 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 13 2026 | 11:42 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping.   The agency also gave more details of remaining volumes to come from a record release of oil from its members' emergency reserves pledged in March, saying 71 million barrels would be made available by the end of February including 15 million barrels of diesel to ease market tightness.   Oil supply will average 105 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, the Paris-based agency, which advises industrialised countries, said in a monthly report, 1.7 million bpd higher than forecast demand. The IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit.

"The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," the agency said in the report.   Oil prices reversed earlier gains after the IEA report was released at 0900 GMT. Brent crude was last down 0.1% at $95.71 a barrel. Also Read

Iran's Guards say they targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain

Iran says it will not allow enriched nuclear material to leave country

US Treasury Secy moved to military housing following Iranian threats

Hormuz will never return to pre-war status, says Iran's chief negotiator

India's renewable energy push saved $100 bn in fuel imports: IEA report

The report follows signs that Gulf oil producers are recovering exports disrupted since the start of the war in late February by using workarounds such as so-called dark crossings through the Strait of Hormuz, where tankers switch off tracking signals to evade attack.   The OPEC+ group, which includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia, pumped 41.23 million bpd of crude in October, OPEC said on Wednesday, up about 2.04 million bpd from September and 97% of the pre-war February volume.

Other Analysts see signs of surplus   Other analysts have also forecast a return to excess supply, despite the lack of a resolution to the Iran war and continuing tanker attacks in the Gulf. JPMorgan last week forecast a global surplus of 1.4 million bpd in October.   High oil prices have also curbed demand this year, helping tip the balance into a surplus. World oil demand is forecast to fall by 2.7 million bpd in 2026 to 102.3 million bpd before rebounding by 2 million bpd in 2027, the IEA said, little changed from its previous forecasts.   As well as rising output from OPEC+, the IEA flagged supply rising from outside the group.

Production from the United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana will rise by 1.6 million bpd this year, the IEA said.   In 2027, global supply is projected to rise by 6.6 million bpd to 108.1 million bpd, led by a further recovery in Gulf output.   Still, the 2027 supply growth forecast is down 1.1 million bpd from last month's report, and the lower outlook partly reflects a downward revision from Iran, the IEA said. Iran is subject to a US blockade that has curbed its oil exports.   For 2027, the IEA sees the supply surplus at about 3.8 million bpd, slightly down from a 3.94 million bpd surplus last month.

item.title: Europe must show readiness to join Ukraine peace talks, says Russia
item.description: Kremlin says no decision has been taken on European participation, despite US claims that Putin agreed to their inclusion ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Europe must show readiness to join Ukraine peace talks, says Russia

Europe must show readiness to join Ukraine peace talks, says Russia Kremlin says no decision has been taken on European participation, despite US claims that Putin agreed to their inclusion

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (centre), in Dublin.

Reuters 4 min read Last Updated : Nov 13 2026 | 11:33 PM IST

Listen to This Article

The Kremlin said on Friday that Europe must show it is ready to contribute to the Ukraine peace process before a decision is made on letting Europeans join the negotiations.   The comment by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov suggests Russia has not yet committed to including Europeans in the next round of talks, despite US negotiators saying on Thursday that President Vladimir Putin had agreed to their participation.   The talks have so far involved Russian,  Ukrainian and US officials, who met in Abu Dhabi this  week for the first time in nine months. Two US envoys then flew to Moscow to meet Putin and later met Ukrainian  President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Dublin.

Asked if peace talks would soon resume with the added participation of Europeans, Peskov said: "Once we understand their genuine intention and readiness to contribute to the peace process, then it will be possible to make a decision on holding dialogue on a Ukrainian settlement in an expanded format."   European involvement would mark a new phase in efforts to end the nearly five-year-old conflict, which has defied attempts by US  President Donald Trump to secure a peace agreement.   Also Read

Foreign businesses seized by Putin help fund Russia's war machine

India's Gulf oil imports surpass Russia for first time since Iran war

Russia, Ukraine reach deal on prisoner swap, but trust gap holds back talks

US attempts new peace push at first Russia-Ukraine talks in nine months

India in talks with Russia, Ukraine on Black Sea food corridors, says MEA

Russia's relations with European powers are dire. European states have armed Ukraine and imposed sanctions on Moscow, and most have shunned direct contact with Putin since he sent troops to Ukraine in February 2022.

Putin said on Thursday the  US must work with its European allies to understand whether they wanted peace or war in Ukraine. Peskov said Moscow would be open to the idea of some form of contacts with Europe before any European participation in peace negotiations, but that no concrete discussions on this had taken place.   Asked how the Kremlin would view French President Emmanuel Macron as a potential interlocutor at peace  talks, Peskov said: "Every hour, reports are appearing that name completely different candidates. So for the time being we are not in a position to say anything specific."   Who Would represent EU?

Peskov declined to comment on the possibility of European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas representing the EU at negotiations. Kallas has frequently questioned Russia's good faith  in the peace process and taken a lead in imposing successive waves of sanctions on Moscow.   She said on Friday it was not up to Russia to say who should represent the EU in peace talks.   "They don't  want anybody strong on the other side because they want to push through their maximum demands," she said. Russia says it wants a full peace settlement, not a ceasefire. Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this week that Moscow wanted to negotiate a broad European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.

Russian and Ukrainian officials said some progress was made at the Abu Dhabi talks, but there was no sign of a major breakthrough on key issues such as territory.   Putin has shown no signs of being ready to moderate his territorial demands, which include a buffer zone in parts of Ukraine which Russia has not formally claimed as its own.   Ukraine has refused Russia's demands to give up territory in the eastern Ukrainian region of Donbas that it has not lost in fighting.                                           EU leaders gather for first AI summit   European Union (EU) leaders gather in Dublin on Friday for their first-ever summit on artificial intelligence (AI), to debate how the bloc can catch up with the US and China and tackle funding issues and other challenges.   The meeting comes amid mounting concerns about a technology that promises to transform industries and societies but has caused alarm in recent months following a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents.  Reuters

item.description: After building Nvidia into an AI chip powerhouse, Huang resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs and a board investigation into alleged foreign intelligence links ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / World News / Broken and shattered: Jensen Huang's last hours as Nvidia Corp's CEO

Broken and shattered: Jensen Huang's last hours as Nvidia Corp's CEO After building Nvidia into an AI chip powerhouse, Huang resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs and a board investigation into alleged foreign intelligence links

Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO following allegations of extramarital affairs and a board probe. | Image: Bloomberg

Bloomberg 6 min read Last Updated : Nov 13 2026 | 10:57 PM IST

Listen to This Article

At the end, Jensen Huang looked broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted. After weeks spent denying the allegations of infidelity and fighting to remain in his job as Nvidia Corp.'s chief executive officer, his surrender late Wednesday night was unconditional. Huang's usual take-charge demeanor had evaporated, according to a person familiar with the situation, and he'd started using phrases like "whatever" and "I don't care."    For the decades he spent building Nvidia into a multitrillion-dollar AI chip behemoth, Huang was famous for his attention to the tiniest of details, from chip architecture to the compensation packages of even the most junior employees at the company. Now, in the eyes of the people in the room, he had given up.

It was a stunningly quick fall for a billionaire and tech titan who two weeks ago was the face of artificial intelligence around the world. With his directness and vigor, he had charmed US President Donald Trump, shaped global tech policy and drawn adoring crowds on his papal-style international tours.    It's hard to imagine the current AI boom happening without Huang, his company and their chips, and it's hard to imagine what it will look like after his fall. As Harvey Jones, chair of the company's board of directors, wrote in an email to employees after Huang's ouster, "Jensen's contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world."

Huang couldn't be reached for comment.    Also Read

Nvidia turmoil links Huang's scandal to AI markets and geopolitics premium

Microsoft 365 outage hits Indian companies, disrupts workplace operations

Zetwerk's Q2 loss widens 43% to ₹88 crore; order book hits record high

In Chinese spy operations, romance can be long game to reach the powerful

Nvidia's next chapter: What its new leaders told staff after Huang's exit

When the news broke in late October that Huang had close ties with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, it looked like he would prevail. The board of directors, dominated by longtime investors, business partners and friends of Huang's, was reluctant to act on the news stories, or even publicly comment on them.   Most of the news coverage tiptoed around the exact nature of the CEO's relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected spy. Huang denied to friends and colleagues that he had been unfaithful to his wife. He'd been denying it when questioned internally since late 2025. In one of his last interviews as CEO, Huang told Bloomberg News that his relationship with Alice Huang was typical of those with Chinese customers and executives. "It was all completely normal and not unusual," he said.

A turning point came last Friday, Nov. 6, when a Financial Times story cited US officials saying that the relationship had been a romantic one.  Soon afterward, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter went to Huang's house to confront him, and Huang confessed. At that point, most of the board still didn't want to take a public stance, but Teter, who is secretary of the board, told them they had to act. The next day, Saturday, the board announced that they would investigate the allegations. A prominent law firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, would lead the inquiry. On Sunday, Huang emailed the entire company, admitting to the affair, apologizing to his family and vowing to "cooperate fully" with the board's investigation.

As the scandal ballooned, there was evidence that it was, perhaps unsurprisingly, drawing Huang's attention away from his extensive duties at the company. As part of Nvidia's idiosyncratic org chart, Huang had around 60 executives at the company who reported to him, a small army by normal management standards. The whole company had to file emails with their top five priorities, which Huang used to check that everyone was working on what he considered most important. Normally he responded to them immediately at all hours of the day and night. In recent days the response times had grown longer.    On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang was also having an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care. This time, the board acted  quickly. Directors assembled remotely on Wednesday, and the meeting lasted late into the night. In the end, Huang was given no choice but to resign, ending his association with the company completely.

The next morning, the board announced Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress would step in as interim CEO. She was quick to try and reassure rattled employees. "I believe deeply in this company and in its future," Kress wrote in an email reviewed by Bloomberg. "More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The Board, staff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you."

She pledged to hold an all-hands meeting on Nov. 18. The following day, Nvidia is due to report results and disclose what Wall Steet analysts predict will be a near doubling of quarterly sales growth.   Now, the board confronts the difficult challenge of finding a replacement for Huang. Some executives considered likely to end up on the shortlist: Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su and Arm Holdings Plc CEO Rene Haas. It's hard to imagine anyone filling all his roles - technologist, executive, marketer, lobbyist, mascot - and the company never bothered to create a traditional succession plan. For better or worse, Nvidia will begin to look more like a regular company going forward, managed in a more regular way.

As for Huang himself, he won't be able to retreat from public life, even if he wants to. In the coming weeks he's expected to testify before Congress, where politicians will ask him about his relationship with Alice Huang and whether it might have put some of the secrets of Nvidia's state-of-the-art chips at risk. According to people who've spoken with him in recent days,  Huang has already taken a penitent turn, castigating himself as a "piece of sh--." He claims not to care what happens to himself at this point. His main concern, he says, is his wife, and not "ruining the lives" of the multiple women now romantically linked to him in the public imagination.                          DoJ yet to conclude Alice Huang was a Chinese spy   US Attorney General Todd Blanche said onThursday that the Justice Department has not yet reached a con-clusion on whether Alice Huang, the Chinese busi-ness woman who had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, was a Chinese spy. Blanche said at a press conference that “of course” the FBI was investi-gating reports that Alice Huang was working for the Chinese government.  Reuters
